findings.title: isTeamAdminOrOwner uses AND instead of OR, blocking team admins
findings.body: Lines 46-48 compute the team permission with `await isTeamAdmin(...) && await isTeamOwner(...)`. The variable name and intent ('admin OR owner') clearly require `||`. As written, a user must be both an admin AND an owner of the team to pass the check; ordinary team admins (and owners who are not also admins) are rejected with FORBIDDEN even though the route is meant to be available to them. This silently breaks the feature for almost all legitimate team users.

findings.title: Any existing attendee can add arbitrary guests
findings.body: Permission is granted to the organizer, team admins/owners, OR any existing attendee (`isAttendee = !!booking.attendees.find(a => a.email === user.email)`). Any booked attendee can therefore inject new emails into the booking, mutate the underlying calendar event, and trigger calendar-invite emails to recipients of their choosing. This is a privilege escalation relative to typical calendar products where only the organizer can grow the attendee list, and it exposes a vector for spam / calendar-invite abuse. The check should be limited to the organizer (and team admins/owners), not all attendees.

findings.title: Handler never checks booking status, event-type policy, or recurrence
findings.body: The handler mutates booking attendees and external calendar events without verifying booking.status (ACCEPTED/PENDING/CANCELLED/REJECTED), without checking booking.endTime (past bookings), without checking eventType.disableGuests, and without handling recurringEventId (a guest added to one instance will not appear in other instances, producing a confusing state). All of these should be rejected up front.

findings.title: Newly-added guests are sent AttendeeScheduledEmail with wrong subject/content
findings.body: In `sendAddGuestsEmails`, every attendee whose email is in `newGuests` receives `AttendeeScheduledEmail` (subject like 'Scheduled: ...', body implying they booked the meeting), while existing attendees receive `AttendeeAddGuestsEmail` (subject 'Guests Added: ...', body 'Added - New guests added to your event'). For a brand-new guest this is the wrong template and is misleading: they did not schedule anything, they were added. Newly-added guests should receive the 'Guests Added' template (or a dedicated 'You were added' template), with a subject and body that reflect that. The current branch also uses the raw `guests` input for comparison, so an existing attendee whose email is duplicated in the input will silently get the 'Scheduled' email instead of the 'Guests Added' one.

findings.title: EventManager is built with the requesting user's credentials, not the organizer's
findings.body: `const credentials = await getUsersCredentials(ctx.user)` and `new EventManager({ ...user, credentials })` use the caller (which may be a team admin or any attendee) instead of the booking organizer. The calendar event being updated belongs to the organizer, and `eventManager.updateCalendarAttendees(evt, booking)` runs with the wrong credentials. When the caller is not the organizer (e.g., a team admin or attendee) the calendar update will silently fail or update the wrong account. Credentials and identity should come from the organizer (e.g., `getUsersCredentials(organizer)` or `new EventManager({ ...organizer, credentials })`).

findings.title: `uniqueGuests` is not actually deduplicated and ignores case
findings.body: The filter on lines 74-78 only removes entries that match an existing attendee's email (case-sensitive `===`) and any entry in the blacklist (lowercased). It does NOT deduplicate the input, so submitting `['a@x.com','a@x.com']` produces two `createMany` rows with identical emails (unless a unique constraint saves it, which is not visible here). It also treats email comparison as case-sensitive even though emails are case-insensitive, so `Guest@x.com` would not be detected as already present if the existing attendee is `guest@x.com`. The misleading name plus the lack of de-duplication can produce duplicate attendee rows and double calendar invites.

findings.title: Guests schema has no min/max length and accepts unbounded input
findings.body: `guests: z.array(z.string().email())` allows any length. With the `addGuests` mutation callable by any attendee of a booking, this is a cheap DoS / abuse vector: a single request can submit thousands of emails, triggering thousands of `createMany` rows, calendar API calls in `EventManager.updateCalendarAttendees`, and an unbounded number of emails in `Promise.all(emailsToSend)`. There is no rate limiting in the handler either. A reasonable cap (e.g., 1-50) should be added at the schema layer.

findings.title: No transaction/locking around attendee creation; double-clicks create duplicates
findings.body: The handler reads the booking, filters out existing emails, then `prisma.booking.update({ data: { attendees: { createMany: { data: guestsFullDetails } } } })`. Two concurrent submissions (e.g., user double-clicks, or two tabs) can both read the booking before either writes, both compute `uniqueGuests` with the same emails, and both succeed in `createMany`, producing duplicate Attendee rows. The whole flow (read -> filter -> createMany -> calendar update -> emails) is not wrapped in a transaction or guarded by any unique constraint on (bookingId, email), so this leaves the booking in an inconsistent state with duplicate attendees and duplicate external calendar invites.

findings.title: 'Additional guests' action is shown for every booking regardless of status
findings.body: The new `add_members` action is appended to `editBookingActions` with no gating on `isUpcoming`, `isConfirmed`, `isPending`, or non-cancelled status. Users can open the dialog for past, cancelled, or rejected bookings; the server-side handler does not block them either. The dialog should at minimum be hidden (or disabled with explanation) for non-actionable booking states, and the server should reject them.

findings.title: `teamId ?? 0` makes isTeamAdmin/isTeamOwner query with team id 0
findings.body: When `booking.eventType?.teamId` is null (a personal/one-on-one booking), the code calls `isTeamAdmin(user.id, 0)` and `isTeamOwner(user.id, 0)`. If any user happens to be an admin/owner of team id 0, they would satisfy this branch on a personal booking they do not own. The team-membership check should be conditional on `booking.eventType?.teamId` actually being set (e.g., `if (booking.eventType?.teamId)` then check, else skip), not fallback to 0.

findings.title: No error handling for calendar update or emails; partial state on failure
findings.body: `eventManager.updateCalendarAttendees(evt, booking)` and `sendAddGuestsEmails(evt, guests)` are the only steps that sync with external systems. `updateCalendarAttendees` is not wrapped in try/catch; a calendar provider failure throws out of the handler after the DB has already been updated with the new attendees. `sendAddGuestsEmails` is wrapped in try/catch but only `console.log`s the error. Result: attendees can exist in the DB without being on the calendar video call and without receiving any notification. Either both side-effects must be transactional/compensating, or the DB write must happen last and roll back on failure.

findings.title: Validation only shows generic 'must be unique and valid' for any failure
findings.body: The local schema is `z.array(z.string().email()).refine(unique)`. Initial state is `[""]`, so the very first click of 'Add' with no input typed fails on the `email()` check (empty string), but the user is shown 'Emails must be unique and valid' — which is not what is wrong. There is also no per-field error and no live validation; the error only appears after clicking submit. Either fix the message to reflect the actual problem, or run validation per row on change.

findings.title: Mutates the `value` prop instead of using a local default
findings.body: `value = value || [];` reassigns the destructured prop in place. With React, props are immutable from the callee's perspective; this either no-ops or, if the consumer passes a non-frozen array, mutates the caller's array on every render. It should be `const values = value ?? [];` (or default via destructuring) so that subsequent `value.map(...)`/`value.push(...)` use a local copy.

findings.title: Organizer email subject assumes attendees[0] exists
findings.body: `organizer-add-guests-email.ts` builds the subject with `name: this.calEvent.attendees[0].name`. If a handler ever calls `sendAddGuestsEmails` for a booking whose `attendees` array is empty (or where the recipient's distinct attendee list excludes any), this throws `Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'name')` and the whole `Promise.all` rejects. Use optional chaining / fallback (e.g., `this.calEvent.attendees[0]?.name ?? this.calEvent.organizer.name`).

findings.title: Emails are sent for the full original `guests` input, including duplicates and rejected entries
findings.body: `sendAddGuestsEmails(evt, guests)` passes the raw request `guests` (not `uniqueGuests`) to determine who is a 'new' guest. If the input contains an existing attendee's email (e.g., user re-submits), that attendee will be classified as 'new' and receive the 'Scheduled' email instead of the 'Guests Added' email. If duplicates appear in the input, the membership check still works on `attendees.map(...)`, so the wrong existing attendee could get the wrong template. Pass the deduped `uniqueGuests` (or a normalized Set of new emails) into the email function.
